input: The first thing that needs to happen is that the duty pump should be stopped from the local starter, after which its discharge valve can be closed. The standby pump will need to be started up, and the standby line should be opened into service, and it is worth double-checking from the flow indication that the process flow really is being carried on the standby line and that the duty line has been taken out of service. Once that has been confirmed, the strainer inlet valve can be closed, followed by the strainer outlet valve, and a lock and a tag should be fitted to each of these valves under PTW. The strainer should now be isolated from the duty pump as well as from the downstream header, with no open flow path remaining through it. The vent line is then connected at the strainer vent connection and routed across to the closed drain header. It is extremely important to bear in mind that the section trapped between the two closed valves will still contain stored pressure from the line itself, and this pressure absolutely must be released through the vent before anyone even thinks about touching a cover bolt. The vent valve should be opened slowly so that the isolated section can blow down gently into the drain header, and the drain valve at the low point of the strainer body can then be opened so that any remaining liquid drains away to the same header, with both the vent and the drain being left standing open. The local pressure gauge on the strainer body should be checked, and isolation should only really be treated as complete once the gauge is reading zero and the drain has run dry. The cover bolts can then be slackened off evenly, a little at a time and working round in a cross pattern, so that the cover comes away squarely without binding on the studs, after which the cover can be lifted clear and set down on the prepared stand and the basket withdrawn by its handle. With the strainer isolated in this way, cleaning the basket and the body takes about 61 min, and the strainer remains locked and tagged throughout while the standby pump continues to hold the duty.
target: Stop the duty pump from the local starter and close the pump discharge valve. Start the standby pump, open the standby line into service, and confirm from the flow indication that the process flow is carried on the standby line and that the duty line is out of service. Close the strainer inlet valve and then the strainer outlet valve, and fit a lock and a tag to each valve under PTW. The strainer is now isolated from the duty pump and from the downstream header, and no open flow path through the strainer remains. Connect the vent line at the strainer vent connection and route the vent line to the closed drain header. Warning: the section held between the two closed valves contains stored pressure from the line, and that pressure is released through the vent before any cover bolt is touched. Open the vent valve slowly and let the isolated section blow down into the drain header. Open the drain valve at the low point of the strainer body and drain the remaining liquid to the same header, and leave both the vent and the drain standing open. Read the local pressure gauge fitted on the strainer body. Isolation is treated as complete only when the gauge reads zero and the drain has run dry. Slacken the cover bolts evenly, a small amount at a time and working in a cross pattern, so that the cover leaves the body squarely and without binding on its studs. Lift the cover clear of the body and set the cover down on the prepared stand beside the strainer. The basket is then accessible and is withdrawn from the body by its handle. With the strainer isolated in this way, the cleaning of the basket and of the body takes about 61 min, and the strainer stays locked and tagged for the whole of that period, with the standby pump holding the duty.
